subject: physical-education
unitTitle: Fitness Literacy I: Training Principles Without Body Metrics
essentialQuestion: What actually makes a body more capable, and how would I notice it?

prompts.prompt: Explain the critical features or key principle of the health-related fitness components and what each one does in your own words.
Demonstrate or fully describe overload, progression, specificity, reversibility, and recovery using a version your body and setting allow. A described or adapted version earns full credit.
Apply frequency, intensity, time, and type as design levers in a new situation and explain the decision or adjustment you made.
Analyze a plausible technique fault, tactical error, or unsafe choice involving monitoring effort by feel, breath, and speech; correct it and explain why.
Connect noticing capability change through what the learner can now do with evaluating fitness claims and products critically and explain how one affects the other.

Present the strongest evidence from the unit task: Design a four-week progression for one self-chosen capability and state how progress will be recognized through tasks the learner can perform — never through weight, size, body composition, or appearance.
Identify one thing you can now do or direct yourself, one adjustment that improved it, and one next goal you set for yourself.

adaptationChoices: The chosen capability may be endurance, strength, mobility, coordination, balance, or a functional task; a learner with a medical restriction designs the progression inside that restriction with guardian input.
accommodationNote: Access supports may change format, pacing, intensity, range, equipment, setting, or response mode without changing the standard being assessed. An adapted or described performance is full credit, not partial credit.
neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, or body-fat percentage.
This task never requires calorie counting or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires disclosing private medical history, a diagnosis, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.
